headline: A rifle jammed at a Hindu temple. Co-workers called.
summary: A 19-year-old drove to a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois on Sunday with a rifle and body armor while thousands were inside for a festival. He waited in the parking lot and left when the gun jammed. Two Taco Bell co-workers called police. He is charged with making a terrorist threat; leaders want it called a hate crime.
cover_answer: No. Telling when someone could get hurt is the rule.
table_question: A friend says he wants to hurt people. Who do you tell?
photo_subject: Sri Venkateswara Swami Temple of Greater Chicago

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: A man drove to a temple in Illinois, a place people go to pray, and he wanted to hurt the people inside. His gun got stuck, like a zipper that won't budge, and two people from his job called the police. The police found him that same day. Nobody at the temple was hurt, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Only if they hear it. A stuck gun, two callers, nobody hurt.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event and reads your face before the words, so the script gives them the stuck gun and the two workmates who called, and ends on nobody hurt. Expect "was it near us?" Illinois, and the temple was fine. Telling a grown-up is the one part they can use.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: A 19-year-old drove to a Hindu temple in Illinois on Sunday with a rifle and body armor. Thousands were inside for a festival. The gun jammed and he left. Two Taco Bell co-workers had heard his plan and called police; he was arrested that day. The school poster had it: see something, say something.
8-12.why: Jam, call, arrest. The poster rule is the mechanism, and it worked.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect, so the script runs one chain: two co-workers heard a plan, they called, police found him that day. The poster rule is the mechanism, and it worked before anyone was hurt. Expect "why did he want to?" Police say his writings were full of hate for non-white people. Say so.

13-17.script: What stopped it: a jammed rifle, or two Taco Bell co-workers who called police? A 19-year-old sat outside a packed Hindu temple in Illinois on Sunday until his rifle jammed. Online slurs against South Asians rose 109% in two years. Second: does calling it a hate crime change anything?
13-17.why: Luck or a phone call, and what the label does. Hold both.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: it failed by luck, a rifle that jammed, and by design, two people who called. The script asks which, then hands them the 109% and the fight over the words hate crime, which leaders want and the charges don't use. Expect "would I have called?" Ask it back and argue honestly.

5-7.a: No. Tattling is about small stuff. When someone could get hurt, you tell a grown-up every time. Those two did, and the police came.

8-12.q: Why did he want to hurt them?
8-12.a: His writings called himself a white supremacist, police say.
He's charged with a terrorist threat and a gun count. A court decides.

13-17.q: What stopped it, the jam or the call?
13-17.a: The jam got him out of the lot. The call got him arrested that day.
Leaders want it charged as one. So far: a terrorist threat and a gun count.

caption:
No. Telling when someone could get hurt is the rule.

A 19-year-old drove to a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois on Sunday with a rifle and body armor while thousands were inside for a festival. He waited in the parking lot and left when the gun jammed. Two Taco Bell co-workers called police. He is charged with making a terrorist threat; leaders want it called a hate crime.

Source: PBS NewsHour

Swipe for what to say at age 6, at 11, and at 17.
